latin.342: Quae enim Deus facit ut judex, ea facit secundum latam a se legem & justitiae normam; quae vero facit ut absolutum habens in creaturas suas ius, ea facit pro liberrimo suo beneplacito, non autem secundum aliquam legem praestitutam, poscente justitia.
latin.343: GAR. Nos hanc rationem urgemus &c. Malum, quod jam a tempore primae transgressionis Adae in omnes ipsius posteros ita derivatur, ut non prius incipiant esse, quam illo malo affici, est ex singulari judicio Dei, sive ex voluntate & consilio Dei tanquam Supremi judicis in poenam peccati illius quod in Adamo praecesserat. Atqui labes Originalis est malum, quod a tempore transgressionis Adae in omnes eius posteros ita derivatur, ut non prius esse incipiant, quam illo malo affici. Labes igitur originalis inest in omnibus Adae posteris ex ratione singularis judicii Dei, in poenam primae illius transgressionis Adae; unde per se consequitur illius imputatio.
latin.344: De minore nemo dubitat. Maioris veritas etiam certa est. Nam cum jam supra demonstratum sit, eam corruptionem moralem in omnes ex Adamo descendentem non posse soli naturae adscribi, nemo causam dicere potest, cur non ad singulare Dei consilium atque judicium confugiendum sit: Quod autem malum est a Deo tanquam justo judice, est sine dubio in poenam alicuius peccati praecedentis. At in ipsis posteris primulum conceptis aut nascentibus non est aliud peccatum, quod praecedat eam labem originalem. Deveniendum est igitur ad ipsius Adae peccatum, propter quod Deus illud malum in posteros descendere voluerit.
latin.345: PLAC. Quid est aliud haec ratio, quam, ut loquuntur, petitio principii? Affertur enim pro argumento illud quod plane idem est cum eo quod versatur in quaestione. itaque negatur major: nec probatur ex eo quod ait vir doctus iam supra demonstratum esse: id enim nusquam demonstratum est, nec, ut arbitror, potest demonstrari. Quanquam si accurate loqui volumus, propagatio corruptionis non soli naturae, sed eius depravationi debet ascribi: quae natura sua contagiosa est ut quod maxime. Potest etiam major distingui: & concedi si malum intelligatur a prima Adae transgressione actuali & habituali diversum; sin minus, negari.
latin.346: Huius ergo corruptionis propagationem in omnes Adami posteros soli naturae vitiosae ascribo, ex qua nihil potest gigni nisi vitiosum. Tu vero eam Deo ascribis imputanti peccatum actuale unius Adami omnibus hominibus, illisque singulis & omnibus corruptionem illam, ut peccatum illud puniat, infligenti. Quod si Deus noluisset, vel primum peccatum actuale primi hominis nobis imputare, quemadmodum caetera eiusdem hominis peccata nobis non imputat; aut si imputatum noluisset punire ea poena, qua peccatum est, ac fons omnium aliorum peccatorum, nasceremur absque peccato incorrupti: cur autem utrumque indidit voluit? Confugitis ad justitiam, quae scilicet exigebat ut peccatum illud actuale, & nobis tot post saecula nascituris imputaretur, & imputatum sic puniretur. Eiusmodi justitiam unde habeatis nescio, nec cur justitia appelletur intelligo, & mihi videtur cum ipsa justitiae notione pugnare. Sed de hac re alibi.
latin.347: Quid, inquiet aliquis, factum ne est igitur absque Dei judicio, eodemque justo, ut vitium illud inhaerens in Adamum invaserit, & ab eo in omnes homines permanarit? Non sane. neque enim aut corrumpi Adamus, aut corruptus suam in posteros corruptionem transfundere Deo vel inscio vel invito potuit. Factum est igitur utrumque Deo sapienter & juste permittente. Cur lapsum Adami permiserit nunc non inquiro. lapsu permisso non potuit Adamus sine miraculo non corrumpi. motu enim posito ponitur necessario motus terminus. posito lapsu e loco superiori in inferiorem, eo finito, quod lapsum est in loco inferiore necesse est esse. Itaque fieri non potuit quin post actualem a Deo aversionem & conversionem ad creaturas Adamus non esset a Deo aversus & ad creaturas conversus. fieri etiam non potuit quin deinceps mala uteretur conscientia, deumque exhorresceret. non erat autem consentaneum ut permisso lapsu Deus rerum naturam turbaret impedito lapsus termino, (si tamen absque contradictionis implicatione impediri potuit,) aut cum productum statim destrueret restituto in pristinum statum Adamo. merebatur autem Adamus suo illo actuali peccato ut a Deo desereretur, nec condonari id peccatum potuit nisi ex gratia ob futuram Jesu Christi satisfactionem & mortem. Itaque corruptio Adami tribuitur justo Dei judicio.

pass_a.342: Placeus finishes the tip: what God does as judge he does by a law he laid down and the norm of justice; what he does by absolute right over creatures he does by free good pleasure, not by some prestablished law with justice demanding it—so absolute right and most just judgment do not sit well together in the imputation claim.
pass_a.343: GAR urges a syllogism: whatever evil is derived from Adam's first transgression into all posterity so that they do not begin to be before being affected by it, is from God's singular judgment as Supreme Judge punishing the preceding sin in Adam. But original stain is exactly such an evil. Therefore original stain is in all Adam's posterity by that singular judgment as punishment of Adam's first transgression—and imputation follows of itself.
pass_a.344: No one doubts the minor; the major is also certain for GAR. Moral corruption descending from Adam cannot be ascribed to nature alone, so one must flee to God's singular counsel and judgment. Evil from God as just judge is punishment of some preceding sin; yet in newly conceived or newborn posterity no other sin precedes original stain—so one must come to Adam's own sin as the reason God willed that evil to descend.
pass_a.345: Placeus calls it begging the principle: the argument assumes what is in question. He denies the major; GAR's claim that it was already demonstrated above is nowhere shown and cannot be. Accurately, propagation should be ascribed not to nature alone but to nature's depravation, which is most contagious. Or distinguish the major: concede if the evil is taken as diverse from Adam's first actual and habitual transgression; otherwise deny.
pass_a.346: Placeus ascribes this corruption's spread through all Adam's posterity to vicious nature alone—from which nothing but the vicious can be begotten. GAR ascribes it to God imputing one Adam's actual sin to all men and inflicting that corruption on each to punish the sin. If God had been unwilling either to impute that first actual sin (as he does not impute Adam's other sins) or, having imputed it, to punish with the punishment that is sin and fountain of other sins, we would be born incorrupt—so why will both? The justice that demanded imputation ages later and such punishment Placeus does not recognize as justice; it fights the very notion of justice. Tip: of this matter elsewhere.
pass_a.347: Someone will ask whether Adam's inherent vice invaded him and flowed into all men without God's judgment, and that a just one. Placeus says no: neither could Adam be corrupted nor, once corrupt, transfer corruption to posterity with God unknowing or unwilling—both were done with God wisely and justly permitting. Why God permitted the fall he brackets for now; the fall being permitted, Adam could not without a miracle fail to be corrupted, for a motion posits its terminus, and a fall from higher to lower leaves what fell in the lower place. After actual aversion from God and conversion to creatures he must stand averse and converted, thereafter using an evil conscience and dreading God. It was not fitting that God, having permitted the fall, disturb nature by blocking the fall's terminus or at once destroy the product by restoring Adam. Adam deserved desertion by that actual sin; pardon only of grace for Christ's future satisfaction and death. Tip: Adam's corruption is ascribed to God's just judgment.

342: For what God does as judge, he does according to a law laid down by himself and the norm of justice; but what he does as having absolute right over his creatures, he does by his most free good pleasure, not according to some law prestablished with justice demanding it.
343: GAR. We urge this reason, &c. The evil which already from the time of Adam's first transgression is so derived into all his posterity that they do not begin to be before they are affected by that evil, is from the singular judgment of God, or from the will and counsel of God as Supreme Judge, for the punishment of that sin which had preceded in Adam. But original stain is an evil which from the time of Adam's transgression is so derived into all his posterity that they do not begin to be before they are affected by that evil. Therefore original stain is in all Adam's posterity by reason of the singular judgment of God, for the punishment of that first transgression of Adam; whence of itself follows its imputation.
344: Of the minor no one doubts. The truth of the major is also certain. For since it has already been demonstrated above that that moral corruption descending into all from Adam cannot be ascribed to nature alone, no one can give a cause why recourse should not be had to the singular counsel and judgment of God: But whatever evil is from God as just judge is without doubt for the punishment of some preceding sin. Yet in the posterity themselves first conceived or being born there is no other sin that precedes that original stain. One must therefore come to Adam's own sin, on account of which God willed that evil to descend into posterity.
345: PLAC. What else is this reason than, as they say, a begging of the principle? For that is brought forward as argument which is plainly the same as what is in question. And so the major is denied: nor is it proved from what the learned man says has already been demonstrated above—for that has nowhere been demonstrated, nor, as I think, can it be demonstrated. Although if we wish to speak accurately, the propagation of corruption ought to be ascribed not to nature alone, but to its depravation: which by its nature is as contagious as can be. The major can also be distinguished: and conceded if the evil be understood as diverse from Adam's first actual and habitual transgression; otherwise denied.
346: I therefore ascribe the propagation of this corruption into all Adam's posterity to vicious nature alone, from which nothing can be begotten except what is vicious. But you ascribe it to God imputing the actual sin of one Adam to all men, and inflicting that corruption on each and all of them so as to punish that sin. But if God had been unwilling either to impute the first actual sin of the first man to us, just as he does not impute the rest of that same man's sins to us; or, having imputed it, had been unwilling to punish it with that punishment which is sin and the fountain of all other sins, we would be born without sin, incorrupt: but why did he will to inflict both? You flee to a justice which of course demanded that that actual sin be imputed also to us about to be born so many ages later, and being imputed be so punished. Whence you have such a justice I do not know, nor do I understand why it is called justice, and it seems to me to fight with the very notion of justice. But of this matter elsewhere.
347: What then, someone will say—was it done without God's judgment, and that a just one, that that inherent vice invaded Adam and from him flowed through into all men? Not at all. For neither could Adam be corrupted, nor once corrupted transfer his corruption into posterity, with God either unknowing or unwilling. Both therefore were done with God wisely and justly permitting. Why he permitted Adam's fall I do not now inquire. The fall being permitted, Adam could not without a miracle fail to be corrupted. For a motion being posited, the terminus of the motion is necessarily posited. A fall from a higher place into a lower being posited, when it is finished what has fallen must be in the lower place. And so it could not be that after actual aversion from God and conversion to creatures Adam would not be averse from God and converted to creatures. It also could not be that thereafter he would not use an evil conscience and dread God. Nor was it fitting that, the fall being permitted, God should disturb the nature of things by hindering the terminus of the fall (if indeed it could be hindered without implication of contradiction), or at once destroy what was produced by restoring Adam to his pristine state. But Adam by that actual sin of his deserved to be deserted by God, nor could that sin be pardoned except of grace on account of the future satisfaction and death of Jesus Christ. And so Adam's corruption is ascribed to the just judgment of God.
